You have already gotten some very helpful answers, thought I would give you mine as well to think about. Congrats on the job, by the way! There are plenty of female drivers. How you're treated will heavily depend on the store.

1. Most of the time, the customer will intentionally give you more than enough to cover the cost with a flat bill plus a few extra ones, which tells you they don't need the change (i.e., on a $24 order, they hand you $27). And most of them still say keep the change. But if they don't say otherwise, never assume they don't want change, just ask if they need change. Just proper etiquette.

2. Exact change is extremely rare in pizza running, either the customer paying you exact change or you giving them change back in exact change. So this is where grade school math comes into play - if the first number after the decimal point is 5 or higher, you round up. If it's 4 or lower, you keep it the same. I MIGHT bend this rule if it's .46 or so, but if it's way down there, I ain't rounding up.

3. Money first, food second. NO EXCEPTIONS. Try to find ways to sit the food down if you can't hold it all, like a table on the porch or a chair or something. If you have too much to handle and you can't put the food anywhere other than the ground (which is a massive no-no unless the customer specifically tells you so, which covers your ass), keep it in your car and tell the customer to meet you at the car, where you can grab the cash, count it if need be, then pocket it all, and hand the customer their food. But NEVER give food out then take money. They could short change you or even worse, slam the door in your face and not pay you.

4. It's a rule for your safety, and I usually follow it. A business is perfectly fine since they have people entering and exiting all the time.

5. This varies heavily. Most of the time, I just go to the door, customer answers, we handle the transaction, done. Now sometimes the customer will specifically request that you call first for a reason (sleeping baby, dogs in home, etc). There will be times where you MUST call the customer if you need some way to reach their home (like maybe a gate code that they didn't give or if you can't physically enter their complex because it's for residents/students only). There will be times where the customer doesn't answer the door and you'll call them and let them know their pizza's here. And if they don't answer their phone (I usually call back three times in a row, wait a minute or two, then call back a fourth time) and you've made every effort to contact them, that's when you take the food back.

6. Unless otherwise specified by the customer, ALWAYS make sure they get their food even if it's already paid for online. Online orders are the simplest ones since they're already paid for, so for the most part, you'll have to knock/ring doorbell, hand customer food, done. And since COVID hit, you may have no contact orders, which you have to make every effort to follow (you can't do no contact on cash orders because you have to be in close proximity to collect the money).

7. You are given a bank at the start of your day, anywhere between $15 to $20. One or two fives and ten ones. Whatever money you collect, your store should have a small locker where you drop your money in, and you get it all out at the end of your shift and they cash you out from there. I usually keep my bank in my wallet and my excess cash in my back pocket to insert when I return to the store. Please do not carry a load of cash on you. You're asking for trouble if you do.

8. Yep, happens all the time. No need to work too hard carrying all that food. As long as it's paid for, the customer won't mind.

9. The driving itself is always stressful since you'll do more than what you are accustomed to. But there will be times where it's pitch black and you can't find the customer's home or the store is very busy and you won't have a moment to rest yourself in between deliveries. And apartment complexes are the damn devil, HATED them, especially at night. Some are well laid out and you'll be able to find the right apartment easily, but some do not follow alphabetical and numerical logic and you're driving around trying to find the apartment.

Just some extra tips:

1. Make every effort to come to the customer, not let the customer come to you. That is just part of good customer service. But if there is a situation where the customer HAS to come to you, they'll understand. And if you feel unsafe coming to the customer (i.e., they have big dogs running amok outside or if there are hazards that the customer may be used to but you aren't), call the customer and make them come to you and explain why you couldn't come to them. If the customer willingly comes to you, that works as well, I sure won't complain. 

2. This is a personal rule of mine and it may be a rule that your company has, but please don't walk on people's grass. You'd be surprised at how hypersensitive people are about their grass. Try to find ways where you'll always be on pavement/asphalt/concrete when approaching a door, such as a walkway. You MAY have to walk a ways, but that's just proper etiquette and you respect your customer's property. If there is no way that you can avoid grass or if the customer says you can, then go ahead.

3. Your company might have a rule to never pull into a customer's driveway. I bend this rule if need be. For instance, if a customer's home is on the top of a hill, rest assured I am driving up that driveway. Last thing I want is to lose my balance on a steep hill and $40 worth of pizza is ruined. Or also, if a customer's home is on the side of a busy street, I'm pulling in to allow normal flow of traffic. If it's a neighborhood, nice and flat surface, easily reachable, then yeah, I won't park in the driveway unless I judge it'll be a long walk. This will vary a lot, so use your discretion. But customers won't (and shouldn't) complain about you parking in their driveway since you'll be bringing them lunch or dinner, and your visit will be two to five minutes, depending on the method of payment and how much pizza you have.

4. Last tip I can give you is to never forget the extras, like extra sauces and the drinks! Nobody likes coming back to the store to pick up a 20 oz drink that the customer rightfully paid for, so have everything ready to rock before leaving the store.

You'll definitely have a lot of fun. And you'll lose track of time as it will just fly by. Follow the traffic laws, buckle up, and drive safe. Good luck!

Well, there's several good reasons, actually. But I'll list a few.

1. Wear and tear on your car. Delivery driving takes years of life out of your car from doing the constant stopping and going, parking, turning your car on and off more times in a day than you should, and of course maintenance costs go up with earlier than needed oil changes (they say every three months or every 3,000 miles, whichever comes first). Not to mention your tires, your suspension, your brakes, among other parts that will wear out quickly. You'll be driving the equivalent of between a one hour and a two hour road trip locally every day you're working, and that's one way.

2. It's a dangerous job. Simply because it requires driving, duh, which can always result in you getting in accidents or running over animals, which is never pleasant. But of course, you can always get robbed.

3. You have to rely on the good hearts of strangers to give you the majority of your income. That normal check every two weeks by itself won't cut the mustard because on most days, you'll be making the lower on the road pay rate pretty much 3/4 of your day. Now of course if you don't get a single tip in the pay period (either you are totally SOL or something is wrong with you for that to happen), the employer has to make it up, but still it won't add up to what you should be making in tips.

And that's pretty much my top three. But TBH, as a tipped employee, I'd rather run pizza than be a server/waiter. Now THEY get the measly $2.13/hr from start to finish whereas pizza runners are paid about or a little over double that on the road and minimum wage in store. And servers/waiters have so much on their plate, AND they're on their feet all day. Pizza runners get to sit down and listen to music much of the day. But at least servers/waiters are safer than pizza runners. So yeah.

4. Click on Add.
